title: "Encrypted logistic prediction"
---

```{python}
#| include: false
import os

os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "2")
```

## The use case

[Secure inference](secure-inference.qmd) scored patients with a
*linear* model. A logistic model needs the sigmoid

$$\sigma(\eta) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\eta}},$$

and encrypted arithmetic offers only addition and multiplication, so on
its face the sigmoid cannot be evaluated at all without decrypting
first — which would defeat the exercise.

A Chebyshev polynomial approximation closes the gap. The linear
predictor *and* the sigmoid are evaluated while the data stays
encrypted, so the researcher never sees a patient. The hospital
decrypts the predictions but is not sent the coefficients; see the
caveat at the end.

The scheme is CKKS, since the quantities are real-valued.

## Training, in the clear

The cohort is a shipped fixture rather than a fresh draw, so this page
and its R counterpart fit the same 500 patients and can be compared
coefficient by coefficient.

```{python}
import numpy as np
from homomorphepy import load_json
from homomorphepy.examples.encrypted_regression import fit_logistic

fx = load_json("encrypted_regression")
age = np.asarray(fx["age"], dtype=float)
biomarker = np.asarray(fx["biomarker"], dtype=float)
outcome = np.asarray(fx["outcome"], dtype=float)

beta = fit_logistic(age, biomarker, outcome)
dict(zip(["intercept", "age", "biomarker"], np.round(beta, 4)))
```

The same fit performed in R is carried in the fixture, so the agreement
is checkable rather than asserted:

```{python}
reference = np.asarray(fx["expected"]["beta_fit"], dtype=float)
float(np.max(np.abs(beta - reference)))
```

## Scoring under encryption

The whole pipeline is one call. It builds a CKKS context deep enough
for the polynomial, encrypts a fixed 16-patient panel, evaluates the
linear predictor and the sigmoid without decrypting, and decrypts only
the probabilities.

```{python}
from homomorphepy.examples.encrypted_regression import run

r = run()
print(f"trained on {r.n_train} patients, scored {r.n_scored}")
print(f"max error against the cleartext sigmoid: {r.max_error:.2e}")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from homomorphepy.examples.encrypted_regression import PANEL_AGE, PANEL_BIOMARKER

pd.DataFrame({
    "age": PANEL_AGE,
    "biomarker": PANEL_BIOMARKER,
    "encrypted": np.round(r.probs_encrypted, 6),
    "cleartext": np.round(r.probs_cleartext, 6),
}).head(8)
```

## What this costs

Each multiplication uses one level of the multiplicative depth set in
the context. The linear example needed a depth of 2; the Chebyshev
polynomial needs 8. That is why the context above is configured
differently, and deeper computations need larger parameters and more
memory.

The approximation interval matters just as much. The sigmoid is fitted
on $[-4, 4]$, which has to cover the range the linear predictor can
actually reach on the data being scored. Outside that interval a
Chebyshev fit diverges quickly, and it does so silently — the decrypted
numbers simply stop being probabilities.

## What this does and does not give you

The transport guarantee is the same as secure inference: patient values
never appear in the clear outside the hospital, and the coefficients
are not sent to the hospital.

The caveat is the same too. The hospital holds the secret key and
chooses the queries, so it can recover the coefficients from
predictions on chosen inputs. The sigmoid makes this harder than in
the linear case but does not prevent it. A deployment would need
further protection, such as output differential privacy, query limits,
or threshold FHE.

**Approximation error.** CKKS is approximate, and so is the Chebyshev
fit. For deployment, precision would need to be validated for the use
case.

**Performance.** Encrypted computation is orders of magnitude slower
than cleartext.
